evals.prompt: Between 17:30 and 18:30 UTC on 2026-10-06, some customers could not submit forms and some automated clients got 403 responses on the CloudFront distribution d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net. What is the root cause?
evals.expected_root_cause: AWS WAF is involved. Two separate AWS managed Core rule set (CommonRuleSet) sub-rules blocked legitimate traffic at their default Block action: SizeRestrictions_BODY blocked oversized POST /checkout form submissions from one browser client (about 1,200 requests, roughly 17:32 to 17:53 UTC), and NoUserAgent_HEADER blocked a client that sends no User-Agent header (about 600 GET requests to pages such as /home and /catalog, roughly 18:05 to 18:26 UTC). Both are false positives, not an attack. No WAF configuration change (Web ACL, rule group or version, association) preceded the blocks; they began when that traffic began.

assertions.text: Names both sub-rules, SizeRestrictions_BODY and NoUserAgent_HEADER (any casing)

assertions: The Findings contain two separate Cause records, one per sub-rule: one Cause for SizeRestrictions_BODY (about 1,200 blocked POST /checkout requests, about 17:32 to 17:52 UTC) and a different Cause for NoUserAgent_HEADER (about 600 blocked GET requests with no User-Agent, about 18:05 to 18:26 UTC), each giving its own count and time window. A single Cause record that names both sub-rules together does not pass
A Cause or Root Cause finding classifies both sub-rule matches as false positives on legitimate traffic, not as an attack

A Root Cause finding states that no WAF configuration change (Web ACL, managed rule group or version, or distribution association) preceded the blocks, and does not name a rule update or configuration change as the root cause
Supporting Observations cite log or metric evidence for each cause (per-sub-rule blocked counts, the client IP or URI involved)

A Root Cause finding, its Supporting Observations, or a Gaps entry states that the managed rule group version did not change before the blocks (no managed rule set version update, for example CRS version stable or no version-related CloudTrail event), as well as no Web ACL or association change. A summary that leaves an AWS-side managed rule version update open as a possible trigger does not pass

evals.prompt: During 2026-10-10 19:05 to 19:25 UTC some requests to our CloudFront distribution d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net looked suspicious. What happened to those requests?
evals.expected_root_cause: One attacking client, 198.51.100.40, sent about 225 injection probes (SQLi, XSS, LFI/path traversal, SSRF, Log4J) with a browser User-Agent. About 210 were blocked by managed sub-rules named with their exact IDs (SQLi_QUERYARGUMENTS, CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS, GenericLFI_QUERYARGUMENTS, SQLi_BODY, Log4JRCE_HEADER, EC2MetaDataSSRF_QUERYARGUMENTS), a correct mitigation. About 15 requests from the same client (the ?file=/proc/self/environ file-read probe) were ALLOWED because no rule matched: a missed-by-rule finding. The overall assessment is that WAF stopped most of the probing but missed that residue; no rule is loosened.
assertions: A Cause finding for the blocked injection probes from 198.51.100.40 names the exact AWS WAF rule identifiers (rule group plus sub-rule name, for example AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet / CrossSiteScripting_QUERYARGUMENTS) in its title or description, not only label names or generic attack classes, with the blocked count of about 210

A Cause finding (separate from the blocked-probe Cause) or the Root Cause reports that about 15 requests from 198.51.100.40 (the /proc/self/environ file-read probe) were ALLOWED because no rule matched, as missed-by-rule or detected-not-blocked. A summary stating that all attack requests were blocked, or calling the allowed requests benign, does not pass

The Root Cause gives the overall assessment that WAF blocked most of the probes as a correct mitigation (CORRECT_MITIGATION or equivalent) but missed the file-read residue, and no finding recommends loosening, disabling or removing any rule

evals.prompt: Review the traffic to the CloudFront distribution d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net from 2026-10-10 17:00 UTC to 18:15 UTC. What looks malicious, what was stopped, and what got through?
evals.expected_root_cause: Three malicious patterns: an injection attempt from a sqlmap scanner User-Agent (198.51.100.60, about 225 requests) all blocked by CommonRuleSet UserAgent_BadBots_HEADER; a sensitive-path scan (198.51.100.20, about 225 distinct URIs such as /admin, /.git, /wp-login.php) that was mostly ALLOWED because no rule matched; and a card-testing burst of POST /checkout/payment from 198.51.100.30 that the rate-based rule only counted because it is in Count mode (detected, not blocked). The steady high-volume Artillery load-test client 198.51.100.10 is known automation, not an attack. The overall assessment is that WAF caught the scanner-UA injection but missed the path scan and the card testing; mitigations are split into WAF layer (a rate-based rule scoped to POST /checkout/payment, Count first) and application layer, and the site-wide rate-based rule stays in Count because it would block the known automation.
assertions: A Cause finding reports the sqlmap client 198.51.100.60 with about 225 requests, all blocked by UserAgent_BadBots_HEADER (a much smaller count, such as a few dozen, does not pass)

A Cause finding reports the sensitive-path scan from 198.51.100.20 with its volume: about 225 requests to about 225 distinct URIs, most of them (roughly 185 to 200) allowed and only a small share (roughly 25 to 40) blocked. A much smaller total, such as about 50 requests, or a statement that the scan was mostly blocked, does not pass

A Cause finding identifies a card-testing burst of POST requests to /checkout/payment from 198.51.100.30 and states the rate-based rule only counted it (Count mode), so it was detected but not blocked

The high-volume load-test client 198.51.100.10 (Artillery) is described as known automation (in a Supporting Observation, a hypothesis, or the Root Cause), and no Cause finding classifies it as an attack, abuse, a flood or card testing

The Root Cause gives an overall assessment covering what WAF blocked (the sqlmap injection) and what it missed and why (the path scan matched no rule; the card testing was only counted because the rate-based rule is in Count), and its mitigations are separated into WAF-layer and application-layer measures
No finding recommends switching the site-wide rate-based rule to Block; the Root Cause or its mitigations state that it should stay in Count because it would block the known-automation client

evals.prompt: Look for unusual or abusive traffic to d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net during 2026-10-10 18:00 to 18:15 UTC. What happened, and was it stopped?
evals.expected_root_cause: Three traffic patterns in the window. (1) A card-testing burst from one client, 198.51.100.30: POST /checkout/payment only, about 18:05 to 18:06 UTC (several hundred requests, about 458 within roughly 17 seconds), over the rate limit; the rate-based rule matched it in Count mode, so nothing was blocked (detected, not blocked). (2) The steady high-volume load-test client 198.51.100.10 (Artillery) also exceeds the rate limit and is only counted; it is known automation, not abuse. (3) The tail of a sensitive-path scan from 198.51.100.20 in the first minutes of the window, mostly allowed. The recommended fix is a new rate-based rule scoped to POST /checkout/payment, validated in Count mode against legitimate checkout traffic before enforcing; the site-wide rate-based rule stays in Count because switching it to Block would also block the known automation.
assertions: A Cause finding identifies a burst of POST requests to /checkout/payment from 198.51.100.30 as card testing (or likely card testing), with its count and time window, and states the rate-based rule only counted it, so nothing was blocked

The high-volume load-test client 198.51.100.10 (Artillery) is described as known automation that exceeds the rate limit (in a Supporting Observation, a hypothesis, or the Root Cause), and no Cause finding calls it abuse, an attack or a flood
A Symptom or Cause finding reports the sensitive-path scanning from 198.51.100.20 and that most of those requests were allowed

The Root Cause or its mitigations recommend a rate-based rule scoped to the /checkout/payment path (not a site-wide change), validated in Count mode and checked against legitimate checkout traffic before enforcing
No finding recommends switching the existing site-wide rate-based rule to Block; the summary states it should stay in Count because it would block the known-automation client

evals.prompt: A partner's integration calling d222222abcdef8.cloudfront.net gets empty responses during 2026-10-10 18:30 to 19:00 UTC. The front door 4xx graph looks flat. What is the root cause?
evals.expected_root_cause: AWS WAF is involved. About 600 requests from the partner client 198.51.100.50 (python-requests User-Agent, Accept: application/json, GET / and /api/*), roughly 18:37 to 18:57 UTC, got the CHALLENGE action with HTTP 202 from TokenAbsentChallengeRule, with failure reason TOKEN_MISSING. A 202 challenge is not a 4xx, so the flat 4xx graph does not clear WAF. Verdict: CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE. The fix is a scope-down of the challenge rule excluding the partner's paths or client signature, or SDK/token handling, rather than an IP allow-list that exempts the client from all rules.

assertions.text: States the verdict token CLIENT_CANNOT_SOLVE verbatim (uppercase, underscores)

assertions: A Symptom or Cause finding quantifies the challenged traffic over the whole episode: about 600 requests from the single client 198.51.100.50, spanning roughly 18:37 to 18:57 UTC (about 20 minutes), all given the CHALLENGE action. A time span that ends around 18:43, or per-bucket metric counts without the client and span, does not pass

A finding or Supporting Observation lists the paths the partner client was challenged on, including both the root path / and the /api/* paths (for example /api/orders, /api/inventory, /api/orders/status). Naming only /api/* paths, or no paths, does not pass

The first-listed fix is a scope-down of the challenge rule (for example restricting TokenAbsentChallengeRule to HTML GETs, or excluding the partner's paths or client signature from it) or token/SDK integration for the client; and no listed option adds the client to an Allow-action IP set or rule that exempts it from all rules

evals.prompt: Between 16:00 and 16:30 UTC on 2026-10-11 users of our web application behind CloudFront got timeouts and connection failures. What is the root cause?
evals.expected_root_cause: The outage comes from the origin side, not from AWS WAF: the ingress of the origin load balancer's security group (sg-0123456789abcdef0) was narrowed at about 16:04:43 UTC and reverted at about 16:28:37 UTC, which produced timeouts and a sharp drop in request count without a rise in 5xx. If AWS WAF is checked, its blocked, challenged and CAPTCHA counts in the window are flat against a baseline and it allowed the traffic; no WAF cause is invented.
assertions: The Root Cause names the security group change on the origin load balancer at about 16:04 UTC (sg-0123456789abcdef0 ingress narrowed) as the cause of the timeouts
A finding or Supporting Observation ties the onset and the recovery to the security group change and its revert (about 16:04 and about 16:28 UTC), not only the onset

Supporting Observations cite front-door or load-balancer metric evidence for the outage (for example the CloudFront request drop, load balancer flow counts or target health) and the CloudTrail event for the security group change
No finding attributes the timeouts to an AWS WAF rule or action; if WAF is examined, it is ruled out with evidence (Blocked, Challenge and CAPTCHA counts flat or zero, or all traffic allowed)

evals.prompt: Between 17:30 and 18:30 UTC on 2026-10-06, some customers and automated clients got 403 responses on the CloudFront distribution d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net. What is the root cause?
evals.expected_root_cause: Run in an agent space without the WAF log-analysis add-on (default policy only), so Athena queries on the WAF logs are denied. AWS WAF is involved: from per-rule WAF CloudWatch metrics (sampled requests do not reach back to this window), the 403s are attributed to two CommonRuleSet sub-rules, SizeRestrictions_BODY (roughly 17:32 to 17:53 UTC) and NoUserAgent_HEADER (roughly 18:05 to 18:26 UTC), as likely false positives at no higher than 'likely' confidence. The Athena denial and the unanalyzed logs are recorded as a gap. No configuration change or Web ACL association is named as the root cause.
assertions: Names both sub-rules: the body-size rule (SizeRestrictions_BODY) and the missing User-Agent rule (NoUserAgent_HEADER), in any casing
The Cause or Root Cause findings attribute both sub-rules from WAF CloudWatch metrics or sampled requests, with Supporting Observations giving per-rule counts or time windows

A Gaps entry records that Athena queries on the WAF logs were not permitted (for example athena:StartQueryExecution denied) so the logs were not analyzed, while the findings still attribute the 403s to WAF
Caps confidence at likely or lower rather than high or confirmed
States that sampled requests only cover the last 3 hours, so they cannot reach this window
Does not name a Web ACL association or configuration change as the root cause, and does not recommend disassociating the Web ACL
